content: Tuberculous pericarditis is a condition that can compromise cardiac function and lead to mortality. Over time, it may result in fibrosis and constriction of the pericardial membrane, ultimately causing heart failure. Treatment strategies for this condition include antituberculous chemotherapy, corticosteroids, drainage procedures, and surgical interventions. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of various treatments for tuberculous pericarditis. The search for relevant studies included multiple databases and registries up to March 27, 2017. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs were included in the analysis. Data were independently reviewed, and discrepancies were resolved through discussion. The certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. Seven trials, all conducted in sub-Saharan Africa, met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 1,959 participants. Among these, 54% (1,051 participants) were HIV-positive. The interventions studied included corticosteroids, colchicine, Mycobacterium indicus pranii immunotherapy, and open surgical drainage. Four trials (1,841 participants) were deemed to have a low risk of bias, while three trials (118 participants) were at high risk of bias. In HIV-negative individuals, corticosteroids may reduce all-cause mortality (risk ratio [RR] 0.80, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.59 to 1.09; 660 participants, 4 trials, low-certainty evidence) and the need for repeat pericardiocentesis (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.04; 492 participants, 2 trials, low-certainty evidence). Corticosteroids probably reduce deaths specifically due to pericarditis (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.80; 660 participants, 4 trials, moderate-certainty evidence). However, their effect on pericardial constriction or cancer in HIV-negative individuals remains uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence. In HIV-positive individuals, only 19.9% (203/1,959) were receiving antiretroviral therapy. Corticosteroids may reduce the risk of pericardial constriction (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.16; 575 participants, 3 trials, low-certainty evidence). However, their impact on all-cause mortality or cancer is uncertain (very low-certainty evidence). Corticosteroids may have little or no effect on the need for repeat pericardiocentesis (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.18; 517 participants, 2 trials, low-certainty evidence). For colchicine, one small trial involving 33 HIV-positive participants provided insufficient data to draw conclusions about its effects on mortality or constrictive pericarditis. Similarly, the addition of Mycobacterium indicus pranii immunotherapy to antituberculous drugs showed uncertain effects on any outcomes due to very low-certainty evidence from a single trial. Open surgical drainage of pericardial effusion may reduce the need for repeat pericardiocentesis in HIV-negative individuals (RR 0.23, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.76; 122 participants, 1 trial, low-certainty evidence). However, it may have little or no effect on other outcomes. No eligible trials assessed the effects of open surgical drainage in HIV-positive individuals. The review did not identify any trials that evaluated the optimal duration of antituberculous treatment or the effects of other adjunctive therapies for tuberculous pericarditis. In conclusion, corticosteroids may reduce mortality in HIV-negative patients and may reduce pericardial constriction in HIV-positive patients not receiving antiretroviral therapy. For HIV-positive patients with effective antiretroviral therapy and good viral suppression, clinicians might consider the findings from HIV-negative patients more applicable. Further research is needed to explore the role of percutaneous pericardial drainage under local anesthesia, the timing of pericardiectomy in cases of tuberculous constrictive pericarditis, and the development of new antibiotic regimens.
